edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina 5 (1844), via Latin Wikisource
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Militiae nomen cum dederis, freno teneris. Incipe tunc ergo dimittere pristina gesta: Luxurias vita, quoniam labor imminet armis. Imperio regis omni virtute parendum, Tempora postrema si vis pertingere laeta. Ille bonus miles, semper exspecta fruenda; Blandire noli tibi, desidias omnino mitte, Ut tuo praeposito cottidie praesto sis, ante Solicitus esto, matutinus signa revise. Cum videris bellum, agonia sume propinqua. Haec gloria regis, militem videre paratum; Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum. Ille parat dona, ille pro victoria laetus Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse. Tu tibi praeterea in Belian parcere noli: Impiger esto magis, ut reddat famam pro morte.
pass_a_gloss: When you have given the name of soldier, you are held by a bridle. Begin then to dismiss former deeds: a life of luxury, because labor with arms is imminent. To the command of the King, obedience is to be given with all virtue, if you wish to reach the last times joyful. He, a good soldier, always expects things to be enjoyed; do not flatter yourself, completely send away idleness, so that you may be present daily to your commander, be solicitous beforehand, revise the signals in the morning. When you see war, take up nearby agony. This is the glory of the King, to see the soldier prepared; the King is present, who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts, he, joyful for victory, suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be. You, moreover, do not spare yourself in respect to Belial: be more energetic, so that he may give fame in exchange for death.

choices.english: he suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be
rejected: he appoints his own attendant to serve you
choices.term: Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse

pass_b_english: Once you've taken on the name of soldier, you're under discipline. It's time to leave your old ways behind - a life of luxury won't cut it when you're facing the hard work of battle. To obey the King's command with all your might is crucial if you hope to make it through the tough times ahead with joy. A good soldier is always on the lookout for what's to come, so don't get complacent and don't let idleness creep in - be ready to report for duty every day, and make sure you're on top of things from the start. Get familiar with the signals, and do it first thing in the morning. When war breaks out, be prepared to face the intense struggle that's coming. The King's glory is in seeing His soldiers prepared for battle, and He's present with those who trust in Him for victory. He's got gifts in store for them, and He's joyful about the victory to come - He's even assigned a personal attendant to each of them. And as for you, don't hold back when it comes to resisting Belial - be more energetic, and you'll earn fame that's worth more than death.

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant theological and semantic shifts that contradict the Locked Latin. 1. 'Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum' is translated in Pass A as 'the King is present, who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope' (preserving the awkwardness of the Latin), but Pass B changes this to 'He's present with those who trust in Him for victory', which adds a relational/theological nuance not present in the text. 2. 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' is translated in Pass A as 'suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be' (literal), but Pass B renders it 'He's even assigned a personal attendant to each of them', which changes the agency and the meaning of 'suspicit' (suspects/looks up) and the structure of the clause. 3. 'in Belian parcere noli' (do not spare/be lenient toward Belial) is rendered in Pass B as 'don't hold back when it comes to resisting Belial', which is a functional interpretation rather than a translation of the specific verb 'parcere' (to spare/be lenient).
reasons: Pass B deviates from the Latin agency and meaning: 'Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum' becomes 'He's present with those who trust in Him for victory' and 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' becomes 'He's even assigned a personal attendant to each of them'.

review.notes: source: 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse', english: 'he suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be'
reasons: Pass A translation 'he suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be' is not faithful to the Latin 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' which literally means 'he suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be' (as per the lemma choices). The phrase 'to be' is ambiguous and not clearly conveyed in the English translation.
